query: Which method can be used for phase stability, microstructure refinement, and property optimization, and why?

generation.hypothesis: A controlled thermomechanical processing method that systematically varies temperature and strain rate under non-equilibrium conditions—while employing in situ XRD and electron microscopy—will enhance phase stability, refine microstructure, and optimize the material properties compared to conventional equilibrium processing.
generation.material_initial_state: A high entropy or compositionally complex alloy with an initial coarse microstructure and equilibrium phase distribution as produced by conventional casting and annealing.
generation.intervention: Application of thermomechanical treatment with a broad temperature range and high strain rates under non-equilibrium conditions, monitored in situ using XRD and electron microscopy.
generation.conditions: Processing under non-equilibrium conditions with systematically varied temperature and strain rate to capture dynamic phase evolution and microstructure refinement.
generation.structural_mediator: Development of finer microstructural features (e.g., refined grain structures, controlled nano-precipitate formation) that serve as mediators of improved mechanical and thermal properties.
generation.mechanism: The high strain rates and varying temperature induce dynamic phase transformations and enhance atomic diffusion and dislocation activity, leading to microstructural refinement and stabilized phases that collectively result in improved mechanical performance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Samples processed via this method will exhibit enhanced phase stability, a significantly refined microstructure (e.g., reduced grain size and more uniform phase distribution), and optimized mechanical properties (such as improved strength and ductility) relative to conventionally processed samples.
generation.baseline: Materials processed under conventional equilibrium conditions (e.g., standard annealing and rolling) with lower strain rates and limited temperature variation, resulting in coarser microstructures and less optimized properties.
generation.boundary: The effectiveness of this method may be limited by the specific alloy composition and the precise window of temperature and strain rate; inappropriate parameter selection could lead to the formation of undesirable phases or defects.
generation.uncertainty: Optimal processing parameters (temperature range and strain rate) for various alloy compositions remain to be fully determined, and the method's effectiveness might vary with different materials.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identical alloy specimens. Subject one set to the proposed controlled thermomechanical process with varied temperature and strain rate while monitoring via in situ XRD and electron microscopy. Process the second set under conventional equilibrium conditions. Compare the phase stability, microstructural features, and mechanical properties (e.g., tensile strength and ductility) between the two sets.
measurements: In situ XRD for phase and structural evolution tracking
Electron microscopy for grain size and microstructure analysis
Mechanical testing (tensile tests) for property optimization assessment
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the thermomechanically processed samples do not exhibit improved phase stability, refined microstructure, or enhanced mechanical properties relative to conventionally processed samples—or if they develop additional unwanted phases—the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

Because modern jet engines require larger and larger parameters, improved creep properties are essential for the aerospace industry. The currently used Ni-based superalloys are reaching their limits, and since the beginning of the 21st century new alloys known as High Entropy Alloys (HEAs) have begun to look attractive [ [1] , [2] ]. HEAs can be regarded as solid solution alloys that contain at least five alloying elements in equal or near equal atomic percentages, and this large number of alloying elements results in maximizing the configurational entropy of the disordered solid solution. However, the microstructure of certain HEAs can include nano-precipitates, ordered solid-solution phases, disordered solid-solution phases, and even amorphous phases [ [1] , [2] ]. Abstract High entropy or compositionally complex alloys provide opportunities for optimization towards new high-temperature materials. Improvements in the equiatomic alloy Al 17 Co 17 Cr 17 Cu 17 Fe 17 Ni 17 (at.%) led to the base alloy for this work with the chemical composition Al 10 Co 25 Cr 8 Fe 15 Ni 36 Ti 6 (at.%). Characterization of the beneficial particle-strengthened microstructure by scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and observation of good mechanical properties at elevated temperatures arose the need of accomplishing further optimization steps. For this purpose, the refractory metals hafnium and molybdenum were added in small amounts (0.5 and 1.0 at.% respectively) because of their well-known positive effects on mechanical properties of Ni-based superalloys. By correlation of microstructural examinations using SEM with tensile tests in the temperature range of room temperature up to 900 °C, conclusions could be drawn for further optimization steps. Keywords: HEA, high entropy alloys, compositionally complex alloys, mechanical characterization
